newsitem.title: INDIA: India greases way for oil exploration drive.
newsitem.headline: India greases way for oil exploration drive.

text.p: India, facing falling crude output and a burgeoning oil price subsidy bill, mapped out a future exploration policy on Friday designed to pay all companies international prices for crude pumped from new fields.

"The government's aim will be to bring a lot of investment into the exploration sector. There is a lot of oil in the ground but not enough funds for investment," Sanjeev Patni, an oil analyst at W.I. Carr brokerage in Bombay, told Reuters.

Indian state owned companies like Oil and Natural Gas Corp (ONGC) and Oil India Ltd (OIL), which produce more than 90 percent of India's oil output, are currently paid only around $11 to $12 a barrel for their crude, while private companies receive international market prices of $22 to $23.
Devi Dayal, a secretary at the Petroleum Ministry, told an industry conference in New Delhi that the national companies should expect equal treatment in future bids for exploration licences.

India is fighting to reverse a slump in crude oil output. Production is expected to fall to 27 million tonnes, about 540,000 barrels per day (bpd), in the year ending March 1997, down from around 31 million tonnes or 620,000 bpd the previous year.
The country is expected to run up an oil import bill of some $9.6 billion in 1996/97 (April-March), and consume around 81 million tonnes or 1.62 million bpd.
India operates a system of administered petroleum product prices, and pays the subsidy out of an oil pool deficit account,
